title: Theater, Circus and Show
description: Ten standalone pieces from the world of live performance: a night backstage, a trapeze family, a stage set, a musical review, a puppet maker, a magician, the history of vaudeville, an understudy, a circus kitchen and a circus doctor.

lessons.title: A Night Backstage
lessons.summary: A volunteer stage manager describes one show night at a small community theater, from her train ride to the final report.
lessons.text:
For six years, I have been the stage manager of the Riverside Players, a community theater in the small town where I live. Nobody in our company is paid. By day, we are teachers, nurses and bus drivers; by night, we are kings, ghosts and lovers. People often ask me what a stage manager does. I make sure that everything happens at the right moment. Here is a single evening.

My day job is in the city, and my commute home takes an hour by train. On show nights, I use the commute to go over my notes, so that when I step off the train, the evening is already clear in my head. I arrive at the theater promptly at five, two and a half hours before the curtain rises.

The first thing waiting for me is paperwork: the sheet that every actor signs on arrival, the report from the night before and a list of repairs. Once, the list of repairs was incomplete, because someone had forgotten to mention a sticking door. That door stuck in the middle of a love scene. Since then, I have refused to accept an incomplete report from anyone.

At six, I walk the stage with our lighting operator. We check, first, that every lamp works and, secondly, that every change looks right. This month we are performing an old ghost story, so the lighting is dark and atmospheric, full of blue shadows and slow changes. We also test the fog machine, which makes the mood even more atmospheric but sets off the fire alarm if we use too much of it.

At seven, the doors open. I like to stand at the back of the center aisle for a moment and watch the audience find their seats. An older couple always asks for seats on the aisle, because the husband has a bad knee.

At twenty-five past seven, I flick the lights in the lobby on and off. In theaters everywhere, that flick of the lights tells people that the show is about to begin. Then our director gives a short speech. First, she asks everyone to turn off their phones. Secondly, she points out the emergency exits. Hardly anyone listens to that part, but the law requires it.

During the show, I sit in a small booth, wearing headphones, and call every cue: lights, sound and fog. A cue must be timely. If a ghost appears one second late, the audience laughs instead of holding its breath. Nobody notices a timely cue, and that is exactly the point.

When the curtain falls, I promptly write my report, lock the doors and walk home. I am always tired, and I am always happy.

Questions:
How does the stage manager use her commute on show nights?
She goes over her notes on the train, so the evening is clear in her head when she arrives.
Why does she refuse to accept an incomplete report?
Once, an incomplete list of repairs did not mention a sticking door, and the door stuck in the middle of a love scene.
What paperwork is waiting for her when she arrives?
The actors' sheet, the report from the night before and a list of repairs are waiting for her.
What does the flick of the lobby lights tell the audience?
It tells them that the show is about to begin.
Why must a cue be timely?
If a ghost appears one second late, the audience laughs instead of holding its breath.

lessons.title: The Flying Kovacs
lessons.summary: A profile of a circus family whose trapeze act has passed through four generations, and of the daughter learning its hardest move.
lessons.text:
For four successive generations, the Kovac family has flown through the air under the roof of a traveling circus. Today the act belongs to Elena Kovac, who is forty-two, her husband, Paul, and their two teenage children. Elena learned from her father, who learned from his mother, who founded the act in a small circus nearly a hundred years ago. Each of those successive generations added something new to the act.

A trapeze act looks like a gamble with death. A performer swings from a bar high above the ring, lets go, turns in the air and is caught by another performer who hangs upside down from a second bar. To the audience, every throw seems like a gamble. To the family, however, it is the opposite of a gamble. Every maneuver has been practiced thousands of times, and nothing is left to chance.

The most important person in the act is the catcher. Paul, who has been the family's catcher for twenty years, compares his job to that of a goalkeeper. "A goalkeeper waits, watches and reacts," he says. "So do I. The flyer makes the beautiful moves, but if I miss, the game is lost." Like a good goalkeeper, he must judge in an instant exactly where the flyer's hands will be.

Not every chapter of the family's history is a happy one. In 1979, Elena's grandfather fell during a show. It was a devastating accident. He suffered a spinal injury, and although he lived for many more years, the spinal damage meant that he never walked again. The family still speaks quietly of that devastating night.

His fall, however, became the catalyst for a lasting change. From that night on, the Kovacs have never performed without a safety net, and their example was a catalyst for other circus families, who soon did the same.

Training is slow and patient. A new maneuver can take a year to learn. Both children began as apprentices at the age of eight. An apprentice starts on a low bar, a few feet above a soft mat, and moves steadily higher as his or her skills grow. Elena believes that an apprentice who climbs too fast learns fear instead of skill.

Their daughter, Sofia, is now fifteen and no longer an apprentice. For two years she has been working steadily on a triple turn, a maneuver that only a few flyers in the world can perform. Last month, during an evening show, she performed it in public for the first time. She let go of the bar, turned three times and reached out her hands. Paul caught her, as he always does. The audience rose to its feet, and in the ring below, Elena was crying with joy.

Questions:
How long has the Kovac family performed in the air?
The family has performed for four successive generations.
Why is the act not really a gamble for the family?
Every maneuver has been practiced thousands of times, and nothing is left to chance.
Why does Paul compare himself to a goalkeeper?
Like a goalkeeper, he waits, watches and reacts, and he must judge where the flyer's hands will be.
What was the catalyst for the family's use of a safety net?
The catalyst was the grandfather's devastating fall in 1979, which left him with a spinal injury.
How does an apprentice in the act begin?
An apprentice starts on a low bar above a soft mat and moves steadily higher.

lessons.title: How to Build a Steam Train
lessons.summary: A volunteer team at a community theater builds a railway station set, with a full-size steam locomotive, in six weeks.
lessons.text:
When the Lakeside Community Theater chose a play set in an old railway station, the set designer, Marcus Bell, faced his biggest challenge yet. The most important scene takes place beside a steam locomotive, and the audience would have to believe that the locomotive was real. This is how his volunteers built it in six weeks.

Every set begins on paper. Marcus works closely with the production planner, a volunteer named Joan, whose job is to keep the work on schedule and within the budget. The planner's rule is simple: every change made after the drawings are approved will incur a cost, in money or in time, and a small theater cannot afford to incur many. So Marcus spends the first week drawing every piece in detail, and Joan checks each drawing against the budget.

The back wall of the station appears to be made of brick. Real bricks would be far too heavy, so the volunteers make them from sheets of foam. For this they use a hot wire cutter, a tool that slides through foam like a knife through butter. With the cutter, one person can make about two hundred bricks in a day. The bricks are glued to wooden panels, and the gaps between them are filled with a gray paste that looks exactly like mortar. From the seats, nobody can tell that the mortar is really colored glue.

The locomotive itself is a frame of steel and wood covered with thin metal sheets. Even without an engine, it weighs about one tonne, or 1,000 kilograms. The whole set weighs nearly three tonnes, so an engineer checked the stage floor before building began. Since the locomotive sits on hidden wheels, four volunteers can push it into place between scenes.

A shiny new locomotive would look wrong in a station that the script describes as old and poor, so the painters add rust. They mix orange, brown and red paint and apply it with a sponge around the wheels and joints, exactly where real rust would form. After a week, the whole machine looks as though it has stood in the rain for fifty years.

For steam, a thin hose runs from a fog machine hidden behind the station wall to the front of the locomotive. When the operator presses a button, white clouds pour from the end of the hose.

Finally, there are ropes everywhere, used to raise the station sign and lower the lamps. In every corner of the stage, the crew keeps a hank of spare rope, wound into a neat loop so that it never knots. "You never know when you'll need a hank of rope," Marcus says.

On opening night, when the steam rolled out and the lamps came down, the audience applauded the set before a single actor had spoken.

Questions:
What does the production planner do?
She keeps the work on schedule and within the budget.
Why does Marcus draw every piece in detail first?
Every change made after the drawings are approved will incur a cost in money or time.
How do the volunteers make the bricks and the mortar?
They cut the bricks from foam with a hot wire cutter and fill the gaps with gray paste that looks like mortar.
How much does the locomotive weigh?
It weighs about one tonne, or 1,000 kilograms.
How does the steam reach the front of the locomotive?
A thin hose carries it from a fog machine hidden behind the wall.

lessons.title: Review: The Pumpkin Mafia
lessons.summary: A newspaper review of an invented musical about a rivalry between two gardeners over the biggest pumpkin at a county fair.
lessons.text:
The Pumpkin Mafia, the new musical at the Garden Street Theater, deals with a subject that small towns take very seriously: the prize for the biggest pumpkin at the county fair. It is also one of the warmest and most enjoyable shows I have seen this year.

The story is easy to follow. Every autumn, a group of older gardeners in the town of Millbrook wins every prize at the fair. They are so powerful that the town calls them the pumpkin mafia. Like a real mafia, they have rules, secrets and a boss: a proud widow named Greta, played by Lorraine Hill with wonderful energy.

Greta's position is threatened when a challenger arrives. Henry Lin, a retired professor of genetics, has just moved to Millbrook to enjoy a quiet life. Using what he knows about genetics, he grows a pumpkin so enormous that the local children call it a mutant. The mutant pumpkin, a huge orange shape that swells a little in every scene, is the funniest thing on the stage, and the young audience around me cheered each time it appeared.

At first, Greta treats the challenger as an enemy, and the first act is full of rivalry. In the second act, however, a horde of beetles descends on the town's gardens. The song in which the horde arrives, with dancers in shiny black costumes, is the highlight of the evening. Against such a pest, rivals cannot afford to fight each other. Greta and Henry join forces, share their knowledge and save the gardens from the pest together.

The pumpkin, of course, is a metaphor. The writers use it as a metaphor for pride, the kind that grows bigger and bigger until it is hard to carry. When Greta and Henry finally agree to enter the fair as a team, the pumpkin no longer matters. The metaphor is never too heavy, though, and the show stays light and quick.

The cast is excellent. Lorraine Hill can articulate a complicated feeling with a single look, and her song about her late husband's garden is quietly moving. As Henry, David Oduya is equally articulate, both in speech and in song; his clear, gentle voice is a pleasure to hear.

The music is not original in style, and one or two of the comic songs go on too long. These are small complaints. The audience on the night I attended was enthusiastic from the first song to the last, and the enthusiastic applause at the end lasted for several minutes. This is an ideal show for families, and I recommend it highly.

Questions:
Why does the town call the group of gardeners the pumpkin mafia?
They are so powerful that they win every prize at the fair, and like a real mafia, they have rules, secrets and a boss.
Who is the challenger, and what does he know about?
The challenger is Henry Lin, a retired professor of genetics.
Why do the children call Henry's pumpkin a mutant?
They call it a mutant because it is so enormous.
What happens when a horde of beetles arrives?
Greta and Henry join forces and save the gardens from the pest together.
What is the pumpkin a metaphor for?
It is a metaphor for pride.

lessons.title: The Woman Behind the Elf
lessons.summary: A profile of a shy puppet maker who has performed for thirty years with a naughty elf puppet that she built and dressed herself.
lessons.text:
For thirty years, Ingrid Moss has shared her stage with a small elf named Pip. Pip is about two feet tall, with pointed ears, a green coat and bright eyes made of jade. He is naughty, quick and funny, and children adore him. Ingrid, by contrast, is a quiet woman who blushes when she is praised.

"As a girl, I could hardly speak in front of my class," she says. "Then, at twelve, I put my hand inside my first puppet and suddenly felt liberated. The puppet could say things I would never dare to say." Even now, after thousands of shows, she still feels liberated each time she lifts the elf from his box.

Ingrid built Pip herself, and she takes great care with every detail. His eyes are carved from real jade, a hard green stone, which she bought in an old jewelry shop. Under stage lights, the jade seems to glow, so that Pip's eyes look alive from the back of the hall.

In Ingrid's shows, Pip plays a prank on her almost every minute. He hides her glasses, steals her sandwich and answers her questions in a silly voice. The naughty elf always apologizes at the end, and the children forgive him, because they secretly hope he will play another prank the next day. "Children love Pip because he is naughty but kind," Ingrid explains. "He breaks small rules, never big ones."

She also sews every garment Pip wears. His coat is made from an old cashmere sweater that once belonged to her mother. Cashmere, she says, is soft and light, so it hangs naturally on a small body, while a cheaper garment would look stiff under the lights.

When Ingrid talks about her craft, she often speaks of a vocabulary. A puppet has no face that moves, so it needs a vocabulary of gestures instead. A tilt of the head means curiosity. A slow turn away means sadness. A quick jump means joy. "Every performer has to learn this vocabulary before saying a single word," she says.

Many young performers have traveled to her small workshop to learn that vocabulary, and Ingrid jokes that she now has disciples. Her first disciple, a young man named Leo, began as her assistant and today runs his own puppet theater in another state. Every winter, he visits her with his own students, and they all watch Pip's show together.

Pip has become valuable in other ways too. A collector once asked for a valuation of the elf, and the valuation came to several thousand dollars. Ingrid only laughed. She will never sell him.

Ingrid is sixty-eight and has no plans to retire. "As long as Pip still wants to play," she says, smiling, "I will be here."

Questions:
What does Pip look like?
He is about two feet tall, with pointed ears, a green coat and eyes made of jade.
How did Ingrid feel when she first put her hand inside a puppet?
She felt liberated, because the puppet could say things she would never dare to say.
What kind of prank does Pip play on Ingrid?
He hides her glasses, steals her sandwich and answers her questions in a silly voice.
Why does Ingrid make Pip's coat from cashmere?
Cashmere is soft and light, so it hangs naturally, while a cheaper garment would look stiff.
Who was Ingrid's first disciple?
Her first disciple was a young man named Leo, who now runs his own puppet theater.

lessons.title: Where You Are Not Looking
lessons.summary: A stage magician explains the principle of guiding an audience's attention, without giving away a single secret.
lessons.text:
People often ask me how my tricks work, and my answer is always a polite refusal. My refusal is not meant to be rude. A trick that is explained becomes a puzzle that has been solved, and nobody holds their breath over a solved puzzle. There is a long disagreement among magicians about how much we should ever tell the public, and I am firmly on the side of saying very little. What I am happy to discuss, however, is the general idea behind almost every trick I do: guiding attention.

Your brain receives far more information than it can handle, so it learns to disregard most of it. Right now, you probably disregard the hum of your refrigerator and the feeling of your shoes on your feet. My work consists of choosing, very carefully, what you will disregard.

Consider a simple moment. I hold up a coin in my right hand and say, "Behold!" It is an old-fashioned word, but magicians love it, because when you hear "behold," your eyes go exactly where I want them. I may also grin at you. A grin draws eyes to the face, and when you grin back, you are no longer watching my left hand.

Attention also follows movement and surprise. A large, slow gesture pulls the eye; a small, quick one goes unseen. People believe their eyes are like cameras that record everything, but they are more like flashlights, lighting up one small area at a time.

The result is a strange kind of certainty. Audiences leave my show with complete certainty that the coin never left my right hand. That certainty is the real trick. On the way home, they speculate about hidden pockets and secret mirrors, and couples often have a friendly disagreement about what they saw. I am glad to let them speculate.

When someone misses the moment that matters, it is not an oversight on their part. Every eye in the room missed it, because I designed the moment so that they would. An oversight on my part, on the other hand, can ruin everything, which is why I practice each trick hundreds of times before I perform it.

Of course, none of this would work if people did not agree to play along. For an hour, my audience chooses to suspend disbelief, and I take that seriously. They suspend their usual doubts, and in return I promise to leave them with wonder, never with real harm.

That promise matters most in one part of my show, in which I take a watch from a volunteer's wrist without the volunteer noticing. On the street, taking a stranger's watch would be a crime, and if the watch were valuable, it could even be a felony. On my stage, it is not a felony, because the watch is always returned within a minute, usually to great applause.

Questions:
What is the magician's answer when people ask how his tricks work?
His answer is always a polite refusal.
What does the brain learn to do with most information?
It learns to disregard most of it.
Why do magicians love the word behold?
When people hear it, their eyes go exactly where the magician wants them.
What certainty do audiences leave with?
They leave with complete certainty that the coin never left his right hand.
Why is taking the volunteer's watch not a felony?
The watch is always returned within a minute.

lessons.title: When Vaudeville Ruled the Stage
lessons.summary: A short history of vaudeville, the variety theater that entertained American families for about fifty years.
lessons.text:
Long before radio, film and television, many families in the United States found their entertainment in vaudeville. For about fifty years, from around 1880 until about 1932, vaudeville theaters filled the main streets of almost every city in the country.

The genesis of vaudeville lies in the rough music halls of the nineteenth century, where men drank, shouted and listened to rude songs. A few clever managers saw a business opportunity. If they offered clean shows, they reasoned, women and children would come too, and twice as many tickets could be sold. That simple idea was the genesis of an industry.

Managers soon joined their theaters into chains, called circuits. The circuits were organized by geographical region: one covered the East, another the Midwest, a third the West. Because of this geographical system, a performer could sign one contract and tour for a whole year, traveling by train from town to town. The rapid conquest of the nation's stages took little more than twenty years, and by the end of that conquest, there was hardly a town without a vaudeville house.

A typical show was a mix of eight or more short acts. An evening might open with a family of jugglers, continue with a singer, a comedian and a trained dog, and end with a cowboy who performed rope tricks. Cowboy acts were especially popular in Eastern cities, where audiences had never seen a real ranch. Many programs also included a skating act, in which a pair of dancers spun across the stage on roller skates. Skating looked dangerous, and audiences loved it.

The best performers became nationally famous. Their names appeared in newspapers across the country, and companies paid them to endorse products such as soap and cough drops. A star might endorse a new brand of piano and see its sales rise nationally within weeks.

Life was much harder for ordinary performers, however. The circuits controlled where they worked and how much they earned, and many complained of exploitation: low pay, long hours and contracts that could be canceled without warning. Some performers formed unions to fight this exploitation. Their efforts did not always succeed, but they set a precedent for the actors' unions that came later. Vaudeville also set another precedent: the idea that one program could offer something for everyone in the family.

When films with sound arrived, audiences moved to the cinema, and vaudeville faded quickly. Yet its influence is everywhere. Many early radio and television stars began on its stages, and the variety shows and talent contests that we watch in the new millennium follow the same old pattern. Vaudeville belongs to another century and, indeed, to another millennium, but its spirit is still with us.

Questions:
What was the genesis of vaudeville?
Managers decided to offer clean shows so that women and children would come too.
How were the circuits organized?
They were organized by geographical region, such as the East, the Midwest and the West.
Why were cowboy acts popular in Eastern cities?
Audiences there had never seen a real ranch.
What did companies pay famous performers to do?
They paid them to endorse products such as soap and cough drops.
What precedent did the performers' unions set?
They set a precedent for the actors' unions that came later.

lessons.title: The Understudy
lessons.summary: An understudy at a community theater housed in an old manor plays the lead in a historical drama when the lead actor falls ill.
lessons.text:
Hannah Price had been an understudy at the Oak Hill Players for three years, and in all that time she had never once gone on stage. An understudy learns another actor's part completely, in case that actor cannot perform. Most nights, Hannah simply sat in the dressing room with a book and waited.

The Oak Hill Players perform in an old manor on the edge of town. The manor was built by a wealthy family more than two hundred years ago, and its great hall, with its tall windows and dark wooden floor, now serves as a small theater with ninety seats.

That autumn, the company was performing a historical drama about the town's early days. The play tells the story of a settler family who arrive in the valley in 1774 and clear a tract of land beside the river. When war breaks out, the father is falsely accused of treason. The family loses its good name and lives in disgrace. The daughter, Abigail, spends the rest of the play proving that her father is innocent of treason. She trusts in providence, but she also works very hard, and in the final scene the family's tract of land and its honor are restored.

Hannah was the understudy for Abigail, the largest part in the play. On the Saturday of the second week, at four in the afternoon, the director called her. The lead actress had a high fever and could not get out of bed. "You're on tonight," the director said.

For an hour, Hannah felt sick with nerves. Then she did what she had practiced for months: she went through the play line by line, in order, from the first scene to the last. She knew every word.

That evening, the manor was full. Among the audience sat the state senator, who represents the town and likes to attend local events in her constituency. Hannah noticed her in the second row and quickly looked away.

From the first scene, the words came easily. When Abigail's father was led away for treason, Hannah's voice shook, and the room fell completely silent. When Abigail finally cleared his name of disgrace, several people in the audience were in tears. Hannah later said that it felt like providence, but the director knew that it was simply months of careful work.

After the curtain call, the whole cast gathered around to congratulate her. The senator came backstage too. She wanted to congratulate Hannah personally, she said, and to tell her that theaters like this one made her constituency a better place to live. Hannah thanked her, and then she went home and slept for eleven hours.

Questions:
What does an understudy do?
An understudy learns another actor's part completely, in case that actor cannot perform.
Where do the Oak Hill Players perform?
They perform in the great hall of an old manor on the edge of town.
What happens to the settler family in the play?
They clear a tract of land, but the father is falsely accused of treason, and the family falls into disgrace.
Why did Hannah go on stage that Saturday?
The lead actress had a high fever and could not get out of bed.
Why did the senator come to congratulate Hannah?
She wanted to praise her and to say that theaters like this one made her constituency a better place.

lessons.title: The Circus Kitchen
lessons.summary: The cook of a touring circus feeds ninety performers from many countries during a season in South Africa.
lessons.text:
When a circus travels, its kitchen travels too. For the past nine years, a friendly cook named Bruno Costa has run the kitchen of the Circus Aurora, which feeds about ninety performers and workers three times a day. This winter, the circus is touring South Africa, and Bruno's kitchen, built inside a long white truck, follows it from city to city.

The performers come from more than twenty countries, so Bruno cooks food from many different cuisines. On Monday there might be pasta from Italy, on Tuesday a stew from Mexico and on Wednesday a curry from India. "Every cuisine is a little piece of home," Bruno says. "When people are far from their families, a familiar meal matters more than you would think." About a third of the company does not eat meat, so every day he also prepares at least two vegetarian dishes. The vegetarian dishes are so good that many of the others choose them too.

Feeding performers who fly through the air is a science of its own. Before a show, nobody wants a heavy stomach while hanging upside down. Bruno therefore serves light meals at lunch, food that is easy to digest: rice, soup, fish and fruit. Heavy food, which takes longer to digest, waits until after the evening show.

Breakfast is the simplest meal. The kitchen offers bread, eggs, yogurt and a long shelf of cereal boxes. The children of the circus families argue happily over which cereal is best. In the early morning, the only sounds in the kitchen tent are quiet voices and the crunch of toast. The children like to crunch their cereal as loudly as they can.

Once a week, Bruno bakes a large vanilla cake for anyone who has a birthday. He makes the vanilla cream from real vanilla, never from a bottle, and the smell fills the whole camp.

In South Africa, Bruno pays in rand, the local currency, and he has learned to compare prices quickly. A large sack of potatoes costs about two hundred rand at the markets he uses. The kitchen truck also needs fuel, so every few days he spends part of his budget on gasoline. On long drives between cities, gasoline can cost more than the vegetables.

In each new city, a governmental health inspector visits the kitchen to check that the floors, the counters and the fridges are clean. Bruno welcomes these governmental visits. "They keep us honest," he says, "and I have nothing to hide." So far this season, his kitchen has passed every inspection.

At night, after the last show, Bruno sits outside his truck with a cup of tea and listens to the performers laughing over their late dinner. For him, that is the sound of a good day's work.

Questions:
Why does Bruno cook food from many different cuisines?
The performers come from more than twenty countries, and a familiar meal reminds them of home.
How many vegetarian dishes does Bruno prepare each day?
He prepares at least two vegetarian dishes every day.
Why does he serve light food before the show?
Light food is easy to digest, and nobody wants a heavy stomach while hanging upside down.
What does Bruno pay in South Africa, and what else does he buy besides food?
He pays in rand, and he also buys gasoline for the kitchen truck.
Why does Bruno welcome the governmental health inspections?
He says they keep the kitchen honest, and he has nothing to hide.

lessons.title: The Doctor Who Joined the Circus
lessons.summary: A former animal doctor now cares for the bodies of circus performers on tour, from aching shoulders to motion sickness.
lessons.text:
Most doctors work in a hospital or a clinic. Ana Reyes works in a small trailer at the edge of a circus tent. For eleven years, she has traveled with the Circus Stella as its doctor, caring for about sixty performers whose bodies are their working tools.

Ana did not start out as a doctor for people. For ten years, she was a vet, treating horses and dogs. "A human is a mammal too," she likes to say. "Every mammal has bones, muscles and a heart that work in much the same way." In her late thirties, she studied medicine and qualified as a doctor for people. Soon afterward, the circus advertised for a doctor, and she got the job.

Her day begins early. Performers often wake with an ache in their shoulders or wrists, and Ana treats each ache before it grows into an injury. She believes that most injuries can be prevented, so before every show she leads the performers through a warm-up routine that she calls activation. During activation, each group of muscles is woken up in turn, from the feet to the neck. "A cold muscle tears," she explains. "A muscle that has gone through activation stretches."

After a show, many performers come to her with swollen knees or ankles. For these, she uses compression: a tight elastic bandage that gently squeezes the joint and reduces the swelling. The members of the skating act, a pair of brothers who spin around the ring on roller skates, are among her most regular patients. Skating at such speed is hard on the knees, and both brothers wear compression sleeves after every performance.

Living close together brings its own problems. When one person catches a stomach bug, half the circus may have it within a week, so Ana insists on careful hand washing in the kitchen and the dressing rooms. Some new performers also suffer from motion sickness on long drives between cities. For motion sickness, she recommends fresh air, a window seat and a few dry crackers.

Water is one of her constant concerns. Performers sweat heavily under hot lights, and many forget to drink enough. Ana teaches them a simple test: if their urine is dark yellow, they need more water; if their urine is pale, they are drinking enough.

Older performers receive extra attention. Once a year, everyone over forty has a cardiac check, because the heart must be strong for this kind of work. Last spring, a cardiac test showed that one of the clowns had high blood pressure. Thanks to the early warning, he changed his diet, took his medicine and is still performing today.

Questions:
What did Ana Reyes do before she became a circus doctor?
She was a vet who treated horses and dogs.
Why does Ana lead the performers through activation before each show?
She believes most injuries can be prevented, and a muscle that has gone through activation stretches instead of tearing.
How does compression help a swollen knee?
A tight elastic bandage gently squeezes the joint and reduces the swelling.
What does Ana recommend for motion sickness?
She recommends fresh air, a window seat and a few dry crackers.
Who receives a cardiac check every year?
Everyone over forty has a cardiac check once a year.
